extracted.intended_audience: comedy writers/performers and readers studying joke technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing or evaluating bait-and-switch comedy: create a setup that raises a concrete expectation (the bait) and then deliver an unexpected but retrospectively sensible reveal (the switch). Covers forms, examples, and what makes the surprise land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Part Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. The Bait: character says something that raises a specific expectation. 2. The Switch: character keeps talking; audience discovers the expectation was wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technique requires a clear division: an explicit or implicit setup that commits the audience to interpretation A, followed by continued speech or action that reframes the setup into interpretation B. The page explains this as the essential anatomy of the joke and gives the general mechanism (audience commitment to A, reveal of B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there a clear setup raising a specific expectation?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a clear setup raising a specific expectation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'bait' should raise a concrete, specific expectation rather than vague implication. A good bait directs the audience toward a single plausible continuation so the switch can subvert it. Example: a phrasing that implies a compliment or a superlative creates expectation of praise or exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the switch deliver something unexpected?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the switch deliver something unexpected?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The switch must actively subvert the expectation established by the bait. The page emphasizes that the character 'keeps talking' and the audience discovers the expectation was wrong. Classic example: Groucho Marx — setup suggests 'actually he's smart', switch reveals 'no, really an idiot.' Unexpectedness is the core of the laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the surprise valid in retrospect (not arbitrary)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the surprise valid in retrospect (not arbitrary)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reveal should make sense when the joke is reconsidered; it must be a reinterpretation that retrospectively fits the bait rather than a random non sequitur. Arbitrary surprises feel cheap/confusing and weaken the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the gap between bait and switch funny (not just confusing)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the gap between bait and switch funny (not just confusing)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be a perceivable, comedic relation between expectation and reveal; if the connection is unclear the audience will be confused instead of amused. Aim for a cognitive leap that produces recognition and amusement, not bafflement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the switch as compact as possible?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the switch as compact as possible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the punch (the switch) brief and economical. The page notes compactness increases impact; long-winded reveals can dilute the effect (although 'long bait-and-switch' / shaggy-dog variants exist, the effective switch itself should usually be concise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-Types / Variation (comparison, comment, long, visual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sub-Types: Bait-and-Switch Comparison; Bait-and-Switch Comment; Long Bait-and-Switch; Visual Bait-and-Switch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are common forms to produce the technique: Comparison flips an expected superlative into an anti-superlative; Comment flips apparent praise into an insult (or vice versa); Long variants build a multi-step setup (shaggy dog stories) before the reveal; Visual variants hide the reveal in framing/camera movement. Choosing an appropriate subtype affects pacing, medium, and how the bait/switch are staged.
